page.title: About · Samantha Paras
page.meta: Samantha Paras spent years in operations and people leadership before software engineering. The thread: notice what's broken, find out why, build something better.
intro.eyebrow: About · Houston, Texas area · open to remote
intro.p1: Before software engineering, I spent years in operations and people leadership. A surprising amount of that work was really systems thinking: finding where a process broke, figuring out why, building a better workflow, documenting it, teaching it, and then adjusting it when real people inevitably used it differently than expected.
intro.p2: Software engineering felt familiar for that reason. The tools changed from warehouse processes, dashboards and SOPs to React components, APIs, databases and Git. But the part I enjoy most stayed remarkably similar: something doesn't work the way it should, I want to understand why, and then I want to make it better.
intro.p3: There wasn't one dramatic moment. I kept learning and moving up in operations, but eventually I'd hit a ceiling and feel like I had more to contribute. I enrolled in TripleTen while working full time, and learning to code was challenging, but my heart felt full in a different way. Seeing something I coded come to life, and knowing it could actually help someone, gave me the fulfillment I'd been looking for.
enjoy.p: I like the point where technical problem-solving and user experience meet. Getting something to technically work is satisfying, but I care just as much about whether someone understands what to do next, whether the interface gets in their way, and whether the thing I built actually solves the problem that made me start it.
devrel.p: Developer Relations interests me because it combines two things I genuinely enjoy: building software and helping people understand how it works. I like troubleshooting something until I understand it, then explaining it clearly enough that someone else doesn't have to struggle through the same problem. It connects directly to my earlier work training people, writing SOPs and turning complicated processes into instructions people could actually use.
smallbiz.p: The gap between a good business and its website can be enormous. I see businesses that are great at what they do, with websites that are outdated, confusing on a phone, hard to navigate or missing the information a customer actually needs. My instinct usually isn't "this looks ugly." It's "this business is making its customers work harder than they need to." That's the kind of problem I'd like to help fix.
work.notice: Notice: I notice recurring friction: inaccurate data, repeated questions, handoffs that break, work that could be easier.
work.ask: Ask: I trace the real cause before fixing symptoms. At Karbach, that meant inventory discrepancies and process gaps. In code, it means checking the state, the response and the data path first.
work.figure: Figure it out: I learn the tool the project needs instead of waiting to feel like an expert.
work.build: Build: At Karbach, I built the dashboards, trackers and SOPs people used to run the day. I want software to be that useful.
work.explain: Explain: I trained people and turned complicated workflows into instructions they could follow. It's a big part of why Developer Relations interests me.
